# KV Cache: Enabling Efficient Long-Context Language Models

## The Computational Bottleneck in Autoregressive Generation

When a large language model generates text, it processes tokens one at a time, with each new token depending on all previous tokens in the sequence. This autoregressive nature means that generating the Nth token requires computing attention scores between that token and every preceding token—a process that scales quadratically with sequence length. Without optimization, this would require redundant recomputation of the same key and value matrices for every generation step, making long-context inference computationally prohibitive.

## What KV Cache Is

The key-value (KV) cache is an optimization technique that stores the key and value matrices from previously processed tokens in memory, eliminating the need to recompute them during autoregressive generation. During the forward pass of each token, the model computes attention projections that produce three components: queries (Q), keys (K), and values (V). Only the new token's K and V projections are computed fresh and appended to the cache. This transforms the attention computation from a quadratic operation over all tokens into a linear operation over just the new token's queries against the cached keys.

## The Computational Bottleneck in Self-Attention

Transformer-based language models generate text through autoregressive decoding—predicting one token at a time, with each prediction conditioned on all previously generated tokens. At the heart of this process lies the self-attention mechanism, which computes relationships between tokens using three vectors: queries (Q), keys (K), and values (V). For each new token position, the model calculates attention scores between its query vector and the key vectors of all preceding positions, then uses these scores to weight the corresponding value vectors.

In naive inference, this attention computation repeats from scratch at every decoding step. When generating token N, the model re-computes Q, K, and V for tokens 1 through N-1—calculations that were already performed when generating tokens 2 through N-1. This redundancy creates quadratic computational complexity with respect to sequence length, making long-context inference prohibitively expensive and slow.

The KV cache addresses this inefficiency by storing computed key and value vectors for previously processed tokens and reusing them in subsequent decoding steps. When generating subsequent tokens, the model retrieves these cached values instead of recomputing them. Only the new token's keys and values are calculated fresh and then appended to the cache.

The first token still requires processing the entire context, but each subsequent token only needs to attend to the cached historical keys and values plus its own new computation.

# KV Cache: Enabling Efficient Long-Context Language Models

## The Computational Bottleneck in Self-Attention

Modern large language models rely on the transformer architecture's self-attention mechanism to process sequences of tokens. In this mechanism, each token in a sequence must attend to every other token to compute attention scores and weighted sums. For a sequence of length *n*, this requires computing attention for each of the *n* tokens against all *n* tokens, resulting in quadratic computational complexity O(*n*²).

During autoregressive generation—the process by which LLMs produce output token by token—the model processes the entire context accumulated so far for each new token it generates. Without optimization, this means that when generating token *t*, the model recomputes attention operations for all previous tokens *1* through *t-1*, even though these computations were already performed during previous generation steps. This redundancy becomes prohibitively expensive as context length grows, making naive attention computation impractical for long sequences.

## How KV Cache Solves This Problem

The key-value (KV) cache addresses this inefficiency by caching the key and value matrices from attention computations so they need not be recomputed. In the attention mechanism, queries (Q), keys (K), and values (V) are projected from input embeddings through learned linear transformations. The attention output for a given token depends on its query vector interacting with all cached key vectors to produce attention weights, which are then applied to the corresponding cached value vectors.
